title: I think they're pulling away
blurb: For when someone has gone quieter and you can feel yourself starting to search for what it means.
entry_signals: I keep checking if they've read it
something feels off and they say it's fine

steps.ask: Before anything else — where are you right now, one to ten?
steps.help: One is barely a flicker. Ten is you cannot think about anything else.

steps.title: Not yet
steps.say:
Nothing useful gets decided from here, and this isn't a discipline problem — above your window of tolerance you aren't choosing between options, you're looking for relief, and at this level you won't care much which one you get.

This flow will still be here at a five. The thing that actually helps is coming back before the spike, not being calmer during it.

steps.ask: Set aside how it feels for a moment. If a friend described this exact situation to you — the same facts, not the same dread — would anything in it worry you?
steps.help: This question comes first on purpose. Everything below is about the gap between what happened and what you concluded. That only helps if nothing is actually wrong.

options.label: Yes — something in it would worry me
No — I think it's mostly happening in me

steps.title: Then this isn't the right tool
steps.say:
If something would worry you about a friend in this position, that is the thing to look at — not whether you're reading it through an anxious lens.

Attachment patterns can amplify a real signal. They do not manufacture one from nothing, and the fastest way to stay somewhere bad is to keep explaining your own alarm to yourself.

Write down what actually happened, in plain language, without interpreting it. Then say it to one person who knows you.
cites: I Cannot Be Okay Until They Change

steps.ask_a: What did they actually do, or not do?
steps.help_a: Only what a camera would have caught. Times, words, actions. Not tone you inferred, not what their silence meant.
steps.ask_b: And what did you take that to mean?
steps.help_b: The conclusion, in the words you've been using in your head.

steps.say: Here they are side by side. Not to say the second one is wrong — it might be exactly right. Only to make it visible that they are two different things, and that you currently have evidence for one of them.

steps.ask: When you noticed, what did you find yourself doing?
steps.help: This is about the move, not about you. Everyone runs one.

options.label: Re-reading things, checking, looking for signs
Getting there first — going quiet, pulling back
Raising the volume so they'd have to respond
Nothing — I've just been sitting with it

steps.ask: What would you need to know to tell the difference between your observation and your conclusion?
steps.help: Something findable. Not "whether they really love me" — something that could actually turn out one way or the other.

steps.ask: Is there a question you could ask that would get you that?
steps.help: Direct, and about them rather than about you. "Has something been going on this week?" gets an answer. "Are you still into this?" asks them to manage your fear.
cites: Taking Your Partner At Face Value

steps.ask: Last one. The thing you want here — is it something you can do, or something they'd have to agree to?
steps.help: Both are fine. They just work differently, and calling one the other is where a lot of frustration comes from.

options.label: Something I can do on my own
Something they'd have to agree to

steps.say: That's the whole thing. Below is what you said, not what I concluded — it's yours to take into the conversation.
